summary:
A Charter newsletter item combining AI-and-work news briefs with an interview with MIT professor Sherry Turkle, author of Artificial Intimacy.

News briefs: California Governor Gavin Newsom signed several AI workplace bills, including the "No Robo Bosses Act," which bars employers from relying on automated decision-making systems to fire or discipline workers and takes effect July 1, 2027. Companion laws ban AI workplace surveillance tools that infer emotional state or collect neural data, and prohibit AI surveillance of employees in workplace bathrooms. A Stanford and King's College London study across 41 countries found generative AI adopters are shifting workforce composition toward senior staff rather than cutting headcount, with junior employees' share dropping nearly two percentage points between 2021 and March 2026 versus comparable non-adopting firms. Employees at leading AI labs increasingly use the generic title "member of the technical staff," up 50 percent in a year, with 39 percent of Anthropic and 31 percent of OpenAI staff listing it on LinkedIn as of last December; a historian warns the vague title "deemphasizes accountability." A McKinsey Global Institute report estimates about 11 million US workers may need to switch occupations by 2035, 3.6 times the historical pace, with only one in seven having a direct pathway into growing jobs.

Turkle interview: AI is reframing work as delegation, creating a loss of ownership, with students unable to recall what their own papers say and medical students bypassing chart review pledges. Lawyers and doctors worry juniors will lose professional formation, the "heartbeat of the work." On remote work, she says people end days on Zoom and Slack without real conversation, and universities suffer from empty halls, classrooms and office hours, eroding community and citizenship. Her remedy for chatbot dependency: make friends, join or organize workplace clubs such as bowling leagues or hiking groups, and re-engage with local community.
